title: Gestational Diabetes Identification and Management Pathway
specialty: Obstetrics, Maternal-Fetal Medicine, and Diabetes Care

evidenceAudit.scope: Pregnant women: screening, diagnosis, glucose targets, treatment escalation, intrapartum glucose control, timing of birth and postnatal testing for gestational diabetes (GDM). Verified against the Saudi MOH Pocket Manual in Obstetrics & Gynaecology (GDM chapter) and NICE NG3; contraindications from US FDA prescribing information. Medicine-pathway restructure on 2026-10-18: medicines regrouped into branches, steps and give-all vs choose-one options; no dose, source or clinical claim was re-checked.

pathophysiology.summary: GDM is hyperglycaemia first recognised in pregnancy. Placental hormones (human placental lactogen, progesterone, cortisol, placental growth hormone) increase insulin resistance in the second and third trimesters; women whose beta cells cannot raise insulin secretion enough develop hyperglycaemia.
keyMechanisms: Maternal glucose crosses the placenta; insulin does not → fetal hyperinsulinaemia → macrosomia, organomegaly, polyhydramnios and shoulder dystocia risk.
After birth the glucose supply stops but fetal hyperinsulinaemia persists → neonatal hypoglycaemia.
Insulin resistance resolves after delivery of the placenta, so most women return to normoglycaemia — but carry a high lifetime risk of type 2 diabetes and recurrence in future pregnancies.
Glucose found before 13 weeks at diabetic levels (fasting above 126 mg/dL, random above 200 mg/dL or HbA1c above 6.5%) indicates overt (pre-existing) diabetes, not GDM.

symptoms: Occasionally thirst, polyuria, recurrent infections (vulvovaginal candidiasis, UTI).
physicalSigns: Fundal height large for dates; polyhydramnios.
Glycosuria on reagent strip (2+ once, or 1+ on 2 or more occasions should prompt testing — NICE).
Risk features: BMI 30 or more, previous baby 4.5 kg or more, previous GDM, first-degree relative with diabetes, high-prevalence ethnicity (NICE).
redFlags: Fasting plasma glucose 7.0 mmol/L or more at diagnosis — start insulin immediately (NICE)
Overt diabetes values at booking (fasting above 126 mg/dL, HbA1c above 6.5%)
Ketosis or vomiting with hyperglycaemia; maternal hypoglycaemia on insulin or glyburide
Macrosomia or polyhydramnios on scan; reduced fetal movements
precipitants: Previous macrosomic baby (4.5 kg or more)
Ethnicity with high diabetes prevalence (includes Middle Eastern populations)

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Diagnostic-range glucose or HbA1c before 13 weeks; persists after birth.

ruleIn.expectedFinding: Overt diabetes: fasting above 126 mg/dL, random above 200 mg/dL or HbA1c above 6.5%. GDM: fasting 95–125 mg/dL.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Separates pre-existing diabetes from GDM at booking (MOH). NICE does not use fasting glucose or HbA1c to screen for GDM.

ruleIn.expectedFinding: 1-hour value 7.8 mmol/L or more → proceed to OGTT.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Below 7.8 mmol/L early in pregnancy: repeat at 24–28 weeks (MOH). NICE uses risk factors instead and does not recommend the challenge test.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: 24–28 weeks (MOH; NICE for risk factors); as soon as possible after booking if previous GDM (NICE)
ruleIn.expectedFinding: MOH: fasting 92–125 mg/dL, 1-h 180 mg/dL or more, or 2-h 153–199 mg/dL — one abnormal value diagnoses GDM. NICE: fasting 5.6 mmol/L or more or 2-h 7.8 mmol/L or more.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Overt diabetes if fasting above 126 or 2-h above 200 mg/dL (MOH). Diagnostic thresholds differ between MOH and NICE — follow the local laboratory pathway.
ruleIn.normalValue: MOH: fasting below 92, 1-h below 180, 2-h below 153 mg/dL; NICE: fasting below 5.6 and 2-h below 7.8 mmol/L

clinicalManagement.title: Screen and diagnose
actions: Booking (before 13 weeks): check fasting/random glucose or HbA1c to detect overt diabetes (MOH).
MOH: 50-g glucose challenge for all; if 7.8 mmol/L or more do a fasting 75-g OGTT.
75-g OGTT at 24–28 weeks; one abnormal value (fasting 92, 1-h 180, 2-h 153 mg/dL) diagnoses GDM (MOH).
Previous GDM: early self-monitoring or OGTT soon after booking, repeated at 24–28 weeks if normal (NICE).
Review in the joint diabetes–antenatal clinic within 1 week of diagnosis (NICE).

clinicalManagement.title: Diet and exercise
actions: Medical nutrition therapy with a dietitian; aim for normoglycaemia, no ketosis and adequate weight gain (MOH).
Daily exercise for 30 minutes, e.g. walking after meals (MOH, NICE).
Teach capillary glucose self-monitoring; targets as in investigations.
Fasting plasma glucose below 7 mmol/L at diagnosis: trial of diet and exercise for 1–2 weeks (NICE).

clinicalManagement.title: Escalate to medicines
actions: NICE: metformin first; insulin if metformin is contraindicated or unacceptable; add insulin if targets still not met.
Fasting plasma glucose 7.0 mmol/L or more at diagnosis: insulin immediately, with or without metformin (NICE). Fasting 6.0–6.9 with macrosomia or polyhydramnios: consider immediate insulin.
MOH: glyburide is a suitable alternative to insulin; insulin total daily dose 0.7 units/kg (1st trimester), 0.8 units/kg (2nd), 0.9 units/kg (3rd).
Insulin: rapid-acting analogues (aspart, lispro) and isophane (NPH) are the preferred insulins in pregnancy (NICE); keep glucose above 4 mmol/L and carry fast-acting glucose.
Antenatal corticosteroids raise glucose: give additional insulin per protocol and monitor closely (NICE).

clinicalManagement.title: Fetal surveillance
actions: Growth scans at 28, 32 and 36 weeks; antenatal fetal testing usually from 32 weeks (MOH).

clinicalManagement.title: Timing and mode of birth
actions: MOH: induction at 39 weeks if glycaemic control is good; earlier if control is suboptimal or comorbidity.
NICE: give birth no later than 40+6 weeks; consider earlier if maternal or fetal complications.
Ultrasound-diagnosed macrosomia: discuss vaginal birth, induction and caesarean (NICE); MOH offers caesarean if estimated fetal weight above 4,750 g.

clinicalManagement.title: Labour and caesarean section
actions: Check blood glucose every 2 hours in established labour; start insulin infusion if above 120 mg/dL, adjusted to the local protocol (MOH). NICE: keep capillary glucose 4–7 mmol/L, using IV dextrose and insulin if not maintained.

MOH sliding scale example: glucose below 70 mg/dL — no insulin, dextrose 5%/saline; below 140 — no insulin, saline or Hartmann's; above 140 — 10 units insulin in 1,000 mL dextrose 5% at 100–125 mL/h, or 0.5–1 unit/h with 100 mL/h dextrose.
Scheduled caesarean: hold the morning dose, start dextrose 5% to avoid ketosis, check glucose hourly, keep 70–190 mg/dL post-operatively (MOH).
Treat promptly if glucose below 50 mg/dL (MOH); stop insulin infusion and give glucose.

clinicalManagement.title: After birth
actions: Stop glucose-lowering medicines after birth in GDM; check fasting and post-meal glucose for 24 h after vaginal birth and 48 h after caesarean (MOH).
Early feeding of the baby; neonatal glucose monitoring for hypoglycaemia (NICE).
Postnatal test: fasting plasma glucose 6–13 weeks (NICE) or 75-g OGTT at 6–12 weeks (MOH); then annual testing.

regimens.indication: GDM not at target after 1–2 weeks of diet and exercise (NICE first-line)
regimens.dose: 500 mg twice daily (or 850 mg once daily) with meals
regimens.frequency: Increase by 500 mg weekly per glucose and tolerance
adjustments: Label dose is for type 2 diabetes; use in pregnancy follows NICE NG3
Stop before iodinated contrast if eGFR 30–60
contraindications: Acute or chronic metabolic acidosis including DKA
regimens.sourceTitle: Metformin hydrochloride prescribing information (US FDA label, DailyMed)

regimens.dose: Total daily dose 0.7 units/kg (1st trimester), 0.8 units/kg (2nd), 0.9 units/kg (3rd)
regimens.duration: Until birth; stop after birth in GDM
adjustments: Titrate to capillary targets; keep glucose above 4 mmol/L
Extra insulin needed with antenatal corticosteroids
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to the insulin or excipients
regimens.sourceTitle: MOH Pocket Manual in Obstetrics & Gynaecology, Saudi Ministry of Health

regimens.dose: 2.5–5 mg once daily with breakfast (1.25 mg if at risk of hypoglycaemia)

learningObjectives: Screen, diagnose and manage gestational diabetes in pregnancy, labour and the postnatal period.
pitfalls: Using HbA1c or fasting glucose to screen for GDM (NICE).
Forgetting extra insulin with antenatal steroids.
Not stopping GDM treatment after birth.
Losing women to follow-up for postnatal glucose testing.
keyPoints: 75-g OGTT at 24–28 weeks; one abnormal value diagnoses GDM (MOH).
Diet and exercise first; escalate within 1–2 weeks if targets not met.
Fasting glucose 7.0 mmol/L or more: insulin straight away.
Induce at 39 weeks if well controlled (MOH); birth by 40+6 (NICE).
Always test glucose after birth: 6–13 weeks then annually.
